relationship: wilderness refuge from communal unfaithfulness
rationale: Jeremiah wishes for a remote wilderness station so that he can leave an unfaithful people. The psalmist likewise wishes to fly away, rest and lodge in the wilderness; the following city scene describes lawlessness and betrayal. Both express a desire for refuge from a corrupt social setting.

relationship: tongue and bow as weapons
rationale: Jeremiah compares the tongue to a stretched bow while describing falsehood. The psalm joins sharpened tongues to a stretched bow and secret shooting. Both portray hostile speech through weapon imagery; they do not identify the same particular attackers.

relationship: distrust within intimate relationships
rationale: Jeremiah warns against trusting a neighbor or brother because betrayal is pervasive. Micah likewise warns against confidence in friends and describes enemies within one's household. The connection concerns the collapse of trust among people normally expected to be close.

relationship: deceitful speech between neighbors
rationale: Jeremiah says friends mock one another and tongues have learned falsehood. The psalm describes empty speech to one's neighbor, deceitful lips and a divided heart. Both locate the failure of truthful speech within ordinary social relationships.

relationship: interest-taking joined to deceit
rationale: Jeremiah places interest upon interest beside deceit upon deceit. The psalm's account of a lawless city likewise names interest-taking and deceit together in its squares. This connection follows the supplied interest-taking wording rather than replacing it with a different description of the people's dwelling.

relationship: falsehood and refusal to know God
rationale: Jeremiah connects multiplying deceit with unwillingness to know the Lord. Hosea's indictment similarly joins the absence of recognition of God to falsehood and other offenses. The shared connection is between social wrongdoing and the failure to acknowledge God.

relationship: divine testing by fire
rationale: The Lord announces that He will put the people through fire and test them because of their evil. Isaiah likewise portrays His action against a disobedient people as burning to purity and removing the lawless. Both use fire for divine dealing with communal corruption.

relationship: gentle speech concealing injury
rationale: Jeremiah calls the tongue a wounding missile and contrasts peaceful words with inward enmity. The psalm says words became softer than oil yet are missiles. Both expose speech that sounds reassuring while functioning as a weapon.

relationship: repeated divine question about vengeance
rationale: Both passages ask whether the Lord will visit these offenses and whether His soul will take vengeance on such a nation or people. The repeated rhetorical question links the new indictment of deceit to the earlier judgment refrain.

relationship: land and animal life affected by judgment
rationale: Jeremiah calls for mourning over emptied wilderness paths as birds and livestock depart. Hosea similarly describes a mourning, diminishing land together with the loss of beasts and birds. Both extend the consequences of human wrongdoing to the inhabited landscape and its animals.

relationship: abandoned cities inhabited by strange creatures
rationale: Jeremiah describes Jerusalem becoming a dwelling of dragons and Judah's cities becoming uninhabited. Isaiah describes another ruined territory whose cities grow thorns and become a dwelling of sirens and ostriches. The parallel is the reversal from human habitation to desolation; the named creatures and territories differ.

relationship: question about the cause of the land's ruin
rationale: Jeremiah asks a discerning hearer to explain why the land has perished and become impassable. Deuteronomy anticipates the nations asking why the Lord treated the land so severely and answers with covenant abandonment. Both frame the ruined land as a question requiring a covenantal explanation.

relationship: abandoned covenant law as the cause of judgment
rationale: The Lord explains the land's disaster by the people's abandonment of His law and refusal to hear Him. Deuteronomy likewise attributes the land's curses to forsaking the covenant and serving other gods. The passages connect judgment to prior obligations that the people rejected.

relationship: repeated accusation of following the evil heart
rationale: Jeremiah 9 describes walking after what pleases the evil heart. Jeremiah 7 similarly says the people did not hear the Lord but walked in the thoughts of their evil heart. The recurrence identifies self-directed desire as a form of refusing divine instruction.

relationship: bitterness and gall as a diet of affliction
rationale: Jeremiah depicts the people's punishment as being fed distresses and made to drink gall-water. The lamenter says he was filled with bitterness and made drunk with gall. Both express suffering through bitter food and drink, with a communal subject in Jeremiah and an individual lamenting voice in Lamentations.

relationship: covenant warning of scattering and the sword
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering among unfamiliar nations and a sword sent after the people. Leviticus's covenant warning likewise combines scattering among nations with the consuming, advancing sword and a desolated homeland. The paired judgments provide a particularly close connection.

relationship: calling skilled mourners
rationale: Jeremiah commands that women skilled in lament be summoned. Amos's announcement of mourning in public places likewise calls people to mourning and to those skilled in wailing. Both portray lament as a communal response involving people practiced in it.

relationship: command to pour out tears for Zion
rationale: Jeremiah calls for a dirge that brings water from eyes and eyelids. Lamentations addresses Zion's walls with the command to bring down torrents of tears and pour out the heart like water. Both make abundant weeping the fitting response to the people's catastrophe.

relationship: Zion's lament over displacement
rationale: Jeremiah hears Zion's lament over misery, shame and the loss of land and dwellings. Lamentations opens with ruined, weeping Jerusalem and deported Judea dwelling among the nations without rest. The passages share communal grief over the loss of a settled homeland.

relationship: same-chapter extension of the call to lament
rationale: After summoning skilled women to begin a dirge, the oracle tells women to teach lament to daughters and neighbors. The reference follows the specific movement from calling practiced mourners to spreading their lament through the community; both passages explicitly concern the women and the dirge.

relationship: death and devastation in public places
rationale: Jeremiah pictures death entering the land and wiping out children outside and young men in the squares. Lamentations describes child and elder lying at the way out, virgins and young men in captivity, and killing by sword and famine. Both portray catastrophe in the community's public spaces without assigning every listed fate to the same group.

relationship: exposed remains without gathering or burial
rationale: Jeremiah 9 depicts people's dead as an example upon the land's surface, left like cut grass without a gatherer. Jeremiah 8 uses the same earth-surface disgrace for exposed bones that will not be mourned or buried. The remains arise in different scenes, but both describe bodies deprived of ordinary care.

relationship: rejection of boasting in human advantage
rationale: Jeremiah forbids boasting in wisdom, strength and wealth. Paul points to the calling of people without worldly wisdom, power or noble birth and says no flesh may boast before God. Both reject human advantage as a sufficient ground for boasting; their lists are not identical.

relationship: scriptural echo of boasting in the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah directs the boaster to understanding and knowing the Lord who acts in mercy, judgment and righteousness. Paul, after describing Christ as wisdom and righteousness from God, introduces as written the instruction to boast in the Lord. The shared redirection of boasting is explicit, without claiming identical wording throughout.

relationship: outward circumcision does not avert judgment
rationale: Jeremiah announces visitation even upon those circumcised in the foreskin. Romans says circumcision benefits the law's practitioner but does not protect a transgressor, and distinguishes outward flesh from the heart. Both deny that the bodily sign by itself settles the person's standing before God.

relationship: circumcision of the heart
rationale: Jeremiah calls Israel's house uncircumcised in heart despite the surrounding discussion of bodily circumcision. Deuteronomy commands circumcision of the hardness of the heart and an end to the stiffened neck. The connection uses the same bodily image for inward responsiveness.

relationship: heavenly bodies and the practices of the nations
rationale: Jeremiah warns Israel not to learn the nations' ways or fear heaven's signs as they do. Deuteronomy warns against being led astray by the sun, moon, stars and heavenly array into serving them. Both distinguish Israel's response to the heavens from the religious practices associated with the nations.

relationship: wood transformed by craftsmen into an idol
rationale: Jeremiah reduces the nations' object of devotion to woodland timber and a carpenter's work. Isaiah follows wood from cutting and practical use to the remainder being fashioned into a god and worshipped. Both expose the manufactured origin of a supposedly divine object.

relationship: precious metal and an immobile handmade object
rationale: Jeremiah describes silver and gold adornment and fastening the object so it does not move. Isaiah describes gold and silver given to a goldsmith and an object that remains where people set it. Both contrast costly workmanship with the object's dependence on human handling.

relationship: idols must be carried and cannot save
rationale: Jeremiah says the objects must be lifted and carried because they cannot take a step, and have no power for good or evil. Isaiah likewise describes people carrying an object that never moves on its own and cannot answer or save. Both deny the carried image independent agency.

relationship: metal idols made by human hands cannot walk
rationale: Jeremiah names worked silver, gold and artisans while stressing that the objects will not walk. The psalm describes the nations' silver-and-gold idols as human handiwork and says their feet will not walk. The parallel concerns material manufacture and the absence of living capability, not the particular trading places or clothing.

relationship: false gods contrasted with the maker of heaven
rationale: Jeremiah pronounces the passing away of gods that did not make heaven and earth. The psalm contrasts the nations' gods with the Lord who made the heavens. Creation marks the decisive difference in both passages.

relationship: creation established by divine wisdom
rationale: Jeremiah joins the making of earth and stretching of heaven to the Lord's strength, wisdom and understanding. Proverbs likewise describes earth founded by wisdom and heaven prepared by good sense. Both attribute the ordered world to divine understanding.

relationship: repeated creation proclamation
rationale: The two passages repeat the earth made by strength, the inhabited world established by wisdom and heaven stretched by understanding. This is a close internal recurrence in the edition's native Jeremiah numbering, linking the creator proclamation across the two oracles.

relationship: clouds and lightning for rain with a wording distinction
rationale: Both passages speak of clouds brought from the earth's extremity and lightning made for rain. The supplied Jeremiah text then says light comes from the treasuries, while the psalm says winds. The shared weather clauses support the comparison without changing either final noun.

relationship: repeated weather proclamation
rationale: Jeremiah 28 repeats the heavenly water, clouds from the earth's end, lightning for rain and light from divine treasuries. In this edition both Jeremiah passages say light. The parallel preserves that wording and follows the repeated account of the creator's activity.

relationship: cast images are false and breathless
rationale: Jeremiah calls the goldsmith's cast works false and says there is no spirit in them. Habakkuk likewise calls the cast object a false appearance and says the plated wood or stone has no breath at all. Both expose the lifelessness of the manufactured object despite its maker's confidence.

relationship: repeated verdict on futile works
rationale: Both passages call the images futile or vain, mocked works that will perish at the time of visitation. The repeated verdict directly follows the same criticism of their manufacture and absence of spirit.

relationship: repeated identification of Jacob's inheritance
rationale: Both passages distinguish Jacob's portion from the lifeless works because the One who formed everything is Himself his inheritance and is named Lord. The connection retains the direction of inheritance stated in these texts.

relationship: divine affliction pictured as a wound
rationale: Jeremiah 10 announces affliction that reveals the people's wound. Jeremiah 37 likewise has the Lord speak of a fracture and painful wound, then identify His blow as discipline for multiplied wrongdoing. Both describe divine judgment through injury imagery; no slinging action is supplied to Jeremiah 10.

relationship: painful wound and lament under discipline
rationale: The lament in Jeremiah 10 names a painful wound and acknowledges it as the speaker's own. Jeremiah 37 repeats the painful-wound language and explains the blow as discipline amid sin and abandonment by friends. The connection is the acknowledged injury of judgment, not an assertion that the voices are identical.

relationship: contrast between a ruined tent and an enlarged tent
rationale: Jeremiah's tent has perished, its coverings are torn and its sons are gone. Isaiah commands widening the tent and curtains because offspring will spread out and settle deserted cities. Both use dwelling and offspring imagery, with the restoration promise reversing the losses lamented in Jeremiah.

relationship: failed shepherds and a scattered flock
rationale: Jeremiah brings together foolish shepherds, failure to seek the Lord and scattering. Ezekiel indicts Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves rather than caring for sheep and explicitly describes the flock scattered without anyone seeking it. Both connect failed leadership with dispersal; Jeremiah's compressed pronouns are not expanded into a new subject.

relationship: calamity from the north against Judah's cities
rationale: The report of a great shaking from the northern land is directed toward the desolation of Judah's cities. Jeremiah's opening vision likewise locates calamity in the north and describes northern kingdoms arrayed against Jerusalem and Judah's cities. The direction, affected region and announced disaster correspond.

relationship: human inability to direct one's own course
rationale: Jeremiah confesses that a person's way does not belong to him and that he cannot make his own course straight. Proverbs says human steps are directed by the Lord and asks how a mortal could understand his ways. Both qualify human control or understanding of one's path.

relationship: request for correction without consuming anger
rationale: Jeremiah asks the Lord to instruct with judgment rather than fury so that the people are not diminished. The psalm asks not to be rebuked in fury or disciplined in anger. Both seek a restrained form of divine correction rather than its devastating intensity.

relationship: shared petition against those who devoured Jacob
rationale: Both prayers ask that divine fury be poured on nations that do not know the Lord or call on His name, because they devoured Jacob and desolated his place or pasture. The sequence of petition, description and reason makes the correspondence especially close.

relationship: public hearing of covenant instruction
rationale: Jeremiah is to speak the covenant's words to Judah's men and Jerusalem's inhabitants. Deuteronomy orders public reading of the law before the gathered people so that they hear and learn to obey. Both make covenant instruction something delivered to the community in its hearing.

relationship: curse upon failure to heed covenant words
rationale: Jeremiah pronounces a curse on the person who will not hear the covenant's words. Deuteronomy pronounces a curse on anyone who does not continue in all the law's words to do them. The shared curse attaches to rejection of the covenant's verbal obligations.

relationship: Egypt as an iron furnace
rationale: Jeremiah recalls the ancestors brought from Egypt, calling it the iron furnace, into a people-and-God relationship. Deuteronomy likewise names Egypt the iron furnace from which God brought Israel to be His people of inheritance. The unusual image and the exodus-to-belonging movement coincide.

relationship: covenant people-and-God formula
rationale: Jeremiah recalls the command to obey together with the promise that they will be His people and He their God. Leviticus states the same reciprocal relationship in the covenant promises. This connection concerns the explicit covenant formula rather than only a general mention of obedience.

relationship: promise of a land flowing with milk and honey
rationale: Jeremiah connects the oath's establishment with the gift of a land flowing with milk and honey. Exodus presents the rescue from Egypt as movement into that same kind of good, spacious land. The earlier promised destination supplies the background to Jeremiah's acknowledgment of the land now given.

relationship: land sworn to the ancestors and given as inheritance
rationale: Jeremiah speaks of establishing the oath sworn to the fathers by giving the land. Exodus names Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the pledge to bring their descendants into the land and give it as inheritance. Both explicitly join ancestral pledge and the gift of land.

relationship: reading the law so that the people do it
rationale: The command to read the covenant words in Judah's cities and outside Jerusalem ends with hearing and doing them. Deuteronomy's public law reading likewise aims at hearing, learning and doing all its words. The shared purpose explains why proclamation is more than recitation.

relationship: same-chapter command and noncompliance
rationale: The short native unit says that they did not do them. The preceding command in 11:6 supplies the antecedent: the covenant words were to be heard and done. This reference makes the stated failure intelligible without reconstructing the absent native verse 11:7.

relationship: covenant broken through serving foreign gods
rationale: Jeremiah describes returning to ancestral wrongdoing, refusing to hear and serving foreign gods, thereby shattering the covenant. Deuteronomy likewise explains the land's judgment through forsaking the covenant and serving gods the people had not known. The correspondence connects religious abandonment with covenant breach.

relationship: refused instruction followed by an unanswered cry
rationale: Jeremiah says the people will cry during inescapable calamity but the Lord will not listen. Wisdom's speech in Proverbs similarly connects prior refusal of her calls and counsel with a later call that will not be heard amid affliction. The pattern corresponds while the literary speakers remain distinct.

relationship: challenge to idols to save in affliction
rationale: Jeremiah 11 asks whether the gods receiving incense will save their worshippers in trouble. Jeremiah 2 likewise challenges the gods the people made to rise and save them when affliction comes. Both expose the failure of the alternative objects of worship at the moment help is needed.

relationship: repeated comparison of gods and altars to city numbers
rationale: Both passages say Judah's gods are as numerous as its cities and connect Jerusalem's streets or exits with sacrifice or incense to Baal. The repeated numerical comparison makes the proliferation of worship explicit; the differing location nouns are retained.

relationship: repeated prohibition of intercession
rationale: In both passages the Lord tells Jeremiah not to pray or petition for this people because He will not listen. Jeremiah 11 specifies their time of affliction, while Jeremiah 7 also forbids approaching on their behalf. The shared command defines the prophet's restricted intercession.

relationship: ritual and prayer do not remove persistent evil
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether prayers and holy meats can remove the beloved woman's evil committed in God's house. Isaiah rejects sacrifices and multiplied supplication when the people's hands are full of blood. Both deny that religious offerings and prayers neutralize ongoing wrongdoing.

relationship: olive-tree judgment imagery
rationale: Jeremiah describes a once beautiful olive tree whose branches become useless under fiery affliction. Romans describes olive branches broken off because of unbelief and warns the remaining hearer not to boast. Both use damaged or removed olive branches to portray judgment within a relationship of belonging, without equating every detail of the images.

relationship: divine planting followed by corrupted response
rationale: Jeremiah 11 names the Lord as the planter who now speaks evil against Israel and Judah for provoking Him with Baal worship. Jeremiah 2 contrasts God's genuine, fruitful planting with the vine's turn to bitterness and foreign character. Both connect an initially good divine planting with a corrupted human response.

relationship: lamb led to slaughter and removal from the living
rationale: Jeremiah compares himself to a guileless lamb led to slaughter while opponents seek to remove him from the land of the living. Isaiah compares the afflicted figure to a sheep led to slaughter and says his life is taken from the earth. The images and threatened removal correspond without identifying the two figures as the same person.

relationship: righteous judge who tests hearts and kidneys
rationale: Jeremiah appeals to the Lord who judges justly and tests kidneys and hearts while entrusting his claim to Him. The psalm asks for judgment according to innocence and names God as tester of hearts and kidneys and a righteous judge. Both ground a plea against wrongdoing in divine scrutiny.

relationship: opposition forbidding a prophet to speak
rationale: Anathoth's men forbid Jeremiah to prophesy in the Lord's name and threaten death. Amaziah forbids Amos to prophesy at Bethel, despite Amos's account of the Lord's commission. Both concern attempts to silence a commissioned prophet; Amos's passage does not contain the same death threat.

relationship: judgment on those plotting against Jeremiah
rationale: The Lord announces sword for the young men and famine for the children of Jeremiah's opponents. Jeremiah 18 places the same family losses in the prophet's plea after describing plots against his life. The outcomes and persecution context correspond, while one passage is God's announcement and the other Jeremiah's petition.

relationship: same-chapter identification and culmination of judgment
rationale: The announcement that no remnant of these opponents will remain completes the judgment on men who threatened Jeremiah and on their households. The earlier verses identify the threat and specify sword and famine. The reference ties the concluding visitation to its identified recipients and cause without enlarging 'of them' to every resident of Anathoth.

relationship: question about the prosperity of the ungodly
rationale: Jeremiah asks why the impious prosper and rejecters flourish while addressing the righteous Lord. Job likewise asks why the ungodly live long in wealth and describes flourishing households and children. Both put the visible success of wrongdoers into a questioning dialogue about justice.

relationship: nearness in speech and distance within
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord is near the people's mouth but far from their kidneys. Isaiah says the people honor Him with lips while their heart is far away. Both contrast outward religious speech with inward distance; each passage's own bodily wording is preserved.

relationship: God's testing and knowledge of the speaker
rationale: Jeremiah appeals to the Lord's knowledge of him and testing of his heart. The psalm begins by saying that the Lord has tested and known the speaker and understood his movements and reasonings. Both ground the address in God's intimate knowledge rather than outward appearance.

relationship: wrongdoing brings mourning to land and animals
rationale: Jeremiah connects the mournful earth, dried grass and vanished livestock and birds with the inhabitants' evil. Hosea's indictment of the land's wrongdoing likewise leads to the land mourning and the decline of beasts and birds. Both explicitly join human evil to ecological devastation.

relationship: betrayal by one's own household
rationale: Jeremiah is warned that even brothers and his father's house reject him and that favorable words should not be trusted. Micah warns against trusting intimate associates and says a man's enemies belong to his own house. Both locate danger inside expected bonds of family confidence.

relationship: abandoned sanctuary and inheritance handed to enemies
rationale: The Lord says He has abandoned His house and inheritance and handed His beloved into enemy hands. The psalm describes rejection of Shiloh's tent, strength handed to captivity and the inheritance disregarded. Both portray the loss of divine protection in terms of dwelling, belonging and enemy control.

relationship: divine rejection of a rebellious people
rationale: Jeremiah portrays the inheritance roaring against the Lord like a lion and states that He hated her. Hosea likewise connects the people's evil and disobedient rulers with divine hatred and expulsion from His house. The common point is rejection following rebellion; Hosea does not repeat the lion image.

relationship: summoning beasts to consume the judged
rationale: Jeremiah commands gathering the field's wild beasts to eat the threatened inheritance. Ezekiel summons birds and beasts to a divine sacrificial feast on the flesh of the defeated. Both use a summons to animal consumption as judgment imagery, but the victims and setting differ.

relationship: God's vineyard reduced to desolation
rationale: Jeremiah says shepherds ruined the Lord's vineyard and turned His desirable portion into wilderness. Isaiah announces the beloved vineyard's removal of protection and abandonment, explicitly identifying it with Israel and Judah. Both depict the devastated people through a vineyard once valued by God.

relationship: devastation that people do not take to heart
rationale: Jeremiah describes the land's ruin and says no one lays it to heart. Isaiah likewise describes Israel handed to plunder, war and burning without understanding or taking it to soul. Both connect destructive judgment with a failure to comprehend its significance.

relationship: the Lord's sword and devastation across the earth
rationale: Jeremiah 12 describes the Lord's sword consuming from one end of the earth to the other, leaving no flesh at peace. Jeremiah 32 describes His judgment with all flesh, the ungodly given to the sword and wounded people lying across the earth. The broad scope and divine judicial agency correspond.

relationship: frustrated sowing and an unprofitable harvest
rationale: Jeremiah contrasts wheat sown with thorns reaped and denies benefit from the allotments. Hosea likewise describes sowing that yields a weak sheaf unable to make flour, with any produce taken by foreigners. Both use failed agricultural return in an oracle of judgment, without making their crop images identical.

relationship: removal of nations under divine judgment
rationale: Jeremiah 12 announces tearing evil neighbors from their land alongside Judah's displacement. Jeremiah 18 describes the Lord's authority to remove and destroy a nation or kingdom, with its response affecting the announced outcome. The shared removal language places judgment beyond Judah alone.

relationship: mercy and resettlement after dispersion
rationale: Jeremiah promises renewed mercy and return to each inheritance after expulsion. Deuteronomy promises mercy, gathering from dispersion and return to ancestral land. The movement from removal to merciful resettlement corresponds, while Jeremiah's surrounding oracle also addresses neighboring peoples.

relationship: outsiders attached to the Lord and welcomed among His people
rationale: Jeremiah promises that neighbors who learn the people's way and swear by the Lord instead of Baal will be built up among His people. Isaiah welcomes foreigners attached to the Lord, serving Him, loving His name and holding His covenant. Both describe inclusion conditioned on attachment to the Lord rather than prior foreign identity.

relationship: nations becoming the Lord's people
rationale: Jeremiah speaks of nations learning the Lord's way and being built up among His people. Zechariah says many nations will take refuge with the Lord and become His people within Zion. Both explicitly envisage nations entering a relationship of belonging to the Lord.

relationship: conditional judgment upon a nation's response
rationale: Jeremiah 12 makes removal and destruction depend on a nation's refusal to return. Jeremiah 18 likewise makes the announced destruction of a nation responsive to whether it turns from evil, and reverses promised good when it disobeys. The conditional structure, not only the vocabulary of destruction, connects the passages.

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the waistcloth sign
rationale: The instruction to put a linen waistcloth around the prophet's waist receives its explicit interpretation when the Lord compares the clinging cloth to Israel and Judah made to cling to Him. The reference connects the particular commanded object and placement to its stated meaning.

relationship: same-chapter enactment of a specific command
rationale: The prophet's acquisition and wearing of the waistcloth carries out the preceding command to acquire it and put it around his waist. The source itself says the action followed the Lord's word; the target supplies that particular word and its object.

relationship: same-chapter concealment and interpretation of the ruined cloth
rationale: The command to hide the waistcloth at the Euphrates in a rock opening leads to its retrieval in a ruined, unusable state and the Lord's comparison with the people's fate. The connection follows the specific object through the sign's action and explicit interpretation.

relationship: same-chapter execution of the concealment command
rationale: The prophet says he went and hid the cloth at the Euphrates as commanded. The target identifies the command, the same river and the rock opening where the object was to be hidden. This connects the stated obedience to its precise instruction.

relationship: same-chapter retrieval instruction and outcome
rationale: The Lord orders a return after many days to take the hidden cloth. The next unit records the return, digging and retrieval, revealing that the cloth is ruined. The particular retrieval links the command with the observed condition that gives the sign its force.

relationship: same-chapter physical sign and its stated meaning
rationale: The retrieved waistcloth is ruined and useful for nothing. The Lord then applies that condition to Judah and Jerusalem's arrogance and disobedience, explicitly saying the people will be like this unusable cloth. This is the text's own interpretation of the sign.

relationship: arrogance brought to ruin
rationale: The Lord announces the ruin of Judah and Jerusalem's arrogance. Proverbs says insolence leads before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall. The connection joins pride with its destructive outcome, while Jeremiah identifies a particular people and divine action.

relationship: same-chapter comparison with the unusable waistcloth
rationale: The oracle says the disobedient, idol-serving people will be like the waistcloth useful for nothing. The earlier retrieval gives the concrete condition to which they are compared: the hidden cloth was ruined and unusable. The explicit comparison supports the reference without inventing a separate sign.

relationship: chosen people intended for renown and glory
rationale: Jeremiah says Israel and Judah were made to cling to the Lord as a renowned people, a boast and a glory, but did not listen. Deuteronomy links the people's chosen status and obedience with being renowned, a boast and glorious. The shared sequence of chosen belonging, intended honor and obedience is particularly close.

relationship: same-chapter proverb explained as judgment
rationale: The saying that every wineskin will be filled with wine is answered by the Lord's announcement that the inhabitants and their leaders will be filled with intoxication and scattered. The target explicitly turns the familiar wineskin saying into a judgment on the people; no earthenware jar is substituted.

relationship: judgment portrayed as collective intoxication
rationale: Jeremiah announces filling the land's inhabitants, rulers, priests and prophets with intoxication. Isaiah addresses Jerusalem as drunk but not from wine after drinking the Lord's cup of anger. Both use intoxication to portray collective catastrophe, with different drinking-vessel imagery in their contexts.

relationship: scattering families without sparing
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering brothers, fathers and sons and declares that the Lord will not spare or pity them so as to withhold destruction. Ezekiel's oracle likewise combines familial catastrophe and scattering with the Lord's refusal to spare or have mercy. The shared pattern is severe communal judgment; the particular family injuries differ.

relationship: warning against self-exaltation before ruin
rationale: Jeremiah tells the hearers not to exalt themselves because the Lord has spoken, within the preceding announcement of destruction. Proverbs warns that insolence goes before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall. The wisdom saying reinforces the oracle's particular warning against pride in the face of judgment.

relationship: responding while light remains
rationale: Jeremiah urges giving God glory before darkness comes and feet stumble while people wait for light. Jesus urges walking while the light remains so that darkness does not overtake the hearers and leave them without direction. Both press for response before the loss of light makes the way uncertain.

relationship: tears over the community's devastation
rationale: Jeremiah warns that the addressed soul and eyes will weep because the Lord's flock was crushed. Lamentations pictures Jerusalem weeping at night with tears on her cheeks and no comforter. The shared grief concerns the devastated community; Jeremiah's wording is not changed into a statement about the prophet's own eyes.

relationship: the fallen crown as loss of honor
rationale: Jeremiah tells the king and those in power to humble themselves because their crown of glory has been taken from their head. Lamentations says the crown fell from the people's head and connects the loss with sin. Both portray humbling and lost honor through the fallen crown, with different addressees.

relationship: Judah's deportation from its land
rationale: Jeremiah declares Judah's deportation complete as the southern cities are shut. The Kings narrative concludes its account of executions at Deblatha by stating that Judah was deported from its land. The shared description of Judah's deportation connects the declaration with the narrative of exile without identifying a particular historical stage for Jeremiah's statement.

relationship: accountability for the Lord's lost flock
rationale: Jeremiah asks Jerusalem where the flock entrusted to her has gone as an enemy approaches from the north. Jeremiah 23 indicts shepherds who scattered and destroyed the Lord's sheep and failed to visit them. Both treat the people as a valued flock whose loss calls those responsible to account.

relationship: invasion likened to labor pains
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether labor pains will seize the addressed city like a woman giving birth when hostile rulers visit. Jeremiah 6 describes the northern attackers and the resulting affliction as labor pains like a woman giving birth. The same childbirth image portrays the distress caused by approaching domination.

relationship: a city's wrongdoing answered with public exposure
rationale: Jeremiah explains the exposure of the city's backside and heels through her great injustice. Nahum announces the exposure of Nineveh's hind parts and the display of her shame to nations. Both use bodily exposure for public humiliation under judgment, without equating the two cities.

relationship: analogies for conduct that cannot produce its opposite
rationale: Jeremiah compares the difficulty of doing good after learning evil with changing skin or a leopard's markings. Jesus says a rotten tree cannot bear good fruit in His teaching about discerning false prophets. Both use an analogy of stable characteristics to expose the problem of expecting good conduct from an evil pattern.

relationship: wind-carried vegetation as dispersal in judgment
rationale: Jeremiah describes the people scattered like brushwood carried by wind into wilderness. The psalm asks God to make enemies like straw before wind and pursue them with a storm. Both use light vegetation blown away to depict people dispersed under divine judgment.

relationship: forgetting the Lord and facing judgment
rationale: Jeremiah assigns the people's portion to disobedience, forgetting the Lord and trusting falsehood. Jeremiah 2 likewise charges the people with forgetting Him and announces judgment against their claim of innocence. Both connect forgetting the Lord with wrongdoing and judgment; the explicit claim of innocence belongs to Jeremiah 2.

relationship: closely parallel exposure of a city's dishonor
rationale: Jeremiah announces uncovering the city's backside over her face so that dishonor is seen. Nahum uses the same striking exposure over the face and shows the city's shame to nations and kingdoms. The literary parallel concerns the image of public disgrace, not an identification of Jerusalem with Nineveh.

relationship: adultery represented by neighing
rationale: Jeremiah 13 joins the city's adultery, neighing and prostitution to its abominations. Jeremiah 5 likewise describes adultery and prostitution, then compares the men to horses neighing after a neighbor's wife. The unusual equine image makes the connection more specific than a general accusation of sin.

relationship: lack of rain in an oracle of judgment
rationale: Jeremiah introduces the Lord's word concerning lack of rain. Amos describes the Lord withholding rainfall and cities searching unsuccessfully for sufficient water. The later details of Jeremiah's drought scene fit this particular prophetic treatment of restricted rain and resulting thirst.

relationship: communal mourning when the land fails
rationale: Jeremiah describes mourning Judea, emptied gates and Jerusalem's cry in the lack of rain. Joel likewise calls for the earth to mourn as grain, wine, oil and trees fail and joy is shamed. Both connect public grief with the collapse of the land's provision, while their immediate disaster descriptions differ.

relationship: unsuccessful search for water
rationale: Jeremiah's emissaries return from wells with empty vessels because they found no water. Amos describes people from several cities coming to one city for water but still not being filled. Both depict an organized search for water that fails to overcome the scarcity.

relationship: failed produce and distressed farmers
rationale: Jeremiah says the land's works failed without rain and farmers were ashamed. Joel addresses farmers and estates amid dried grain, failed harvest and diminished trees. Both present agricultural failure together with the distress of those dependent on the fields.

relationship: animals deprived of pasture
rationale: Jeremiah describes deer abandoning their young because there is no pasture. Joel describes cattle weeping for lack of pasture and sheep disappearing. The connection concerns animals suffering the failure of their food supply; abandonment of young is specific to Jeremiah's image.

relationship: animals suffering the loss of sustenance
rationale: Jeremiah's wild donkeys draw in wind and their eyes fail because there is no grass. Joel describes wilderness vegetation consumed and animals looking up because water outlets dried up. Both extend the land's failure to animals dependent on its sustenance, without making the causes or behaviors identical.

relationship: appeal for help for God's own sake despite sin
rationale: Jeremiah acknowledges many sins standing against the people but asks the Lord to act for His own sake. The psalm likewise asks for compassion, rescue and forgiveness for the glory of God's name. Both seek help for God's own sake while acknowledging wrongdoing; the psalm explicitly names His name.

relationship: prayer against apparent estrangement from God's people
rationale: Jeremiah addresses Israel's saving hope but asks why He seems like a sojourner or one turning aside to lodge. The psalm asks why God rejected His flock and urges remembrance of the congregation and Zion where He encamped. Both appeal from apparent withdrawal to the established relationship between God, people and dwelling.

relationship: appeal to the apparently sleeping deliverer
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether the Lord is like a sleeping man or a man unable to save, then pleads that He not forget the people bearing His name. The psalm asks why the Lord sleeps and forgets affliction, then calls Him to arise and redeem for His name's sake. The images and sequence of the plea closely correspond.

relationship: God now remembers the people's injustices
rationale: Jeremiah announces divine displeasure and says God will now remember their injustices. Hosea likewise says the Lord will not accept the people's sacrifice and will now remember their injustices and punish their sins. The repeated remembrance formula marks an impending accounting rather than acceptance.

relationship: repeated restriction of the prophet's prayer
rationale: The Lord tells Jeremiah not to pray for good things for this people. Jeremiah 7 similarly forbids prayer, requests for mercy and approaching on their behalf. Both restrict the prophet's intercession in the face of the people's persistent wrongdoing.

relationship: rejected offerings and supplication
rationale: Jeremiah says fasting will not secure a hearing and burnt offerings or sacrifices will not please the Lord. Isaiah likewise rejects the multitude of sacrifices and refuses to hear multiplied supplication from bloodstained hands. Both deny that religious activity itself averts judgment on an unrepentant people.

relationship: false assurances of peace
rationale: Jeremiah reports prophets promising freedom from sword and famine and peace in the land. Jeremiah 23 describes prophets speaking from their own hearts who promise peace and no evil to those rejecting the Lord's word. Both expose reassuring prophetic messages that contradict the announced judgment.

relationship: unsent prophets presenting false visions as divine speech
rationale: The Lord denies sending or speaking to Jeremiah's false prophets and names false visions and divinations. Ezekiel likewise describes vain visions and divinations presented as the Lord's word by people He did not send. Both distinguish the divine name claimed by the speakers from their actual lack of commission.

relationship: death announced for an unsent prophet
rationale: Jeremiah 14 announces death for prophets who falsely promise safety though the Lord did not send them. Jeremiah 35 provides the particular case of Hananiah, declared unsent, sentenced to die that year and then reported dead. The case parallels the judgment on false prophecy; it does not establish famine as Hananiah's cause of death.

relationship: Jerusalem's dead left without burial
rationale: Jeremiah describes the people and their families thrown into Jerusalem's thoroughfares through sword and famine, with no one burying them. The psalm likewise describes corpses and blood around Jerusalem with no one to bury the dead. The connection is the burial catastrophe; the psalm calls its dead God's servants, while Jeremiah describes recipients of false prophecy.

relationship: unceasing tears for the shattered daughter of the people
rationale: Jeremiah commands tears day and night without ceasing because the daughter of the people has been crushed. Lamentations similarly commands Zion's walls to bring down tears day and night without pause and to pour out the heart like water. The shared time, command and communal grief make the connection direct.

relationship: sword and famine as paired forms of suffering
rationale: Jeremiah encounters the sword's wounded in the plain and famine's pain in the city. Lamentations compares those wounded by the sword with those wounded by famine. Both set these two forms of suffering together, although Lamentations also judges one condition better than the other.

relationship: frustrated expectation of peace and healing
rationale: Both passages describe an expectation of peace with no good result and a time of healing answered by distress. Jeremiah 14 says turmoil and Jeremiah 8 says haste in the final clause. The repeated structure supports the reference while preserving that wording difference.

relationship: confession of the people's and fathers' wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah acknowledges the people's sins and their fathers' injustices before the Lord. The psalm likewise confesses sin with the fathers and acts of lawlessness and injustice. Both combine present confession with acknowledgment of the ancestral pattern.

relationship: appeal to God's name and covenant in catastrophe
rationale: Jeremiah asks for restraint for the Lord's name and remembrance of His covenant. The psalm likewise asks God to remember the reproach against His name, not forget the needy and look upon His covenant. Both appeal to the existing relationship as the ground for intervention.

relationship: creator and giver of rain contrasted with worthless gods
rationale: Jeremiah denies that the nations' idols can bring rain and directs hope to the One who made all things. Acts calls hearers from worthless worship to the living maker of heaven and earth, whose witness includes rain and fruitful seasons. Both connect rain to the creator; Acts's immediate scene concerns a crowd attempting to worship the apostles as gods.

relationship: Moses as an effective intercessor contrasted with present refusal
rationale: Jeremiah says that even Moses standing before the Lord would not turn His disposition toward this people. Exodus records Moses pleading for Israel and the Lord being appeased concerning the announced calamity. The earlier successful intercession explains the force of naming Moses in the present refusal.

relationship: Samuel as a heard intercessor contrasted with present refusal
rationale: Jeremiah names Samuel alongside Moses when declaring that even their standing before God would not secure acceptance. Samuel's narrative records the people asking him to keep crying for them and the Lord hearing him. That established intercessory role gives the contrast its particular significance.

relationship: repeated assignment to death, sword and deportation
rationale: Jeremiah 15 assigns people to death, sword, famine or captivity. Jeremiah 50 uses the same distribution formula for Egypt, naming death, deportation and sword. The repeated form and overlapping outcomes correspond; famine is not included in the target's list.

relationship: fourfold divine retribution with differing lists
rationale: Jeremiah announces four kinds of vengeance involving sword, dogs, wild beasts and birds. Ezekiel announces four evil retributions involving sword, famine, evil beasts and death. Both explicitly organize divine judgment in four kinds and share sword and beasts, but their fourfold lists are not treated as identical.

relationship: Manasseh's acts in Jerusalem as grounds for Judah's judgment
rationale: Jeremiah attributes the people's distress among kingdoms to Manasseh son of Hezekiah and what he did in Jerusalem. Kings likewise connects Judah's removal with Manasseh's sins and the innocent blood with which he filled Jerusalem. The named king, location and stated causal connection coincide.

relationship: rhetorical questions about an unpitied city
rationale: Jeremiah asks who will spare Jerusalem, be afraid for her or turn back for her peace. Nahum asks who will lament miserable Nineveh or provide consolation. Both frame the city's isolation under judgment through questions about the absence of compassionate response.

relationship: turning away and going backward
rationale: Jeremiah 15 addresses a people who turned away from the Lord and will go backward. Jeremiah 7 similarly describes refusal to hear, following the evil heart and going backward instead of forward. Both use reversed movement to describe the people's response to the Lord.

relationship: bereavement as communal judgment
rationale: Jeremiah describes dispersion, bereavement and destruction among the people because of their evils. Hosea likewise announces bereavement and explicitly describes children reared and exposed to piercing. Both include bereavement within communal judgment, with the affected children named explicitly in Hosea.

relationship: multiplied widowhood amid national loss
rationale: Jeremiah describes widows multiplying and calamity falling suddenly on a young man's mother. Lamentations speaks for a community made fatherless whose mothers are like widows. The shared family loss connects the prophetic warning with the communal lament, without repeating Jeremiah's numerical comparison or timing.

relationship: midday sunset and mourning
rationale: Jeremiah pictures a bereaved mother's sun setting while the day is still at its middle. Amos likewise announces the sun setting at midday and joins daytime darkness to mourning for a beloved one. Both use premature darkness to intensify the portrayal of catastrophic grief.

relationship: prophetic lament over being born into distress
rationale: Jeremiah laments to his mother that he was born to litigation, dispute and curses. Jeremiah 20 likewise curses the day and announcement of his birth and asks why he left the womb to see labor, pain and shame. The connection concerns the burden of the prophet's life; no lending or borrowing is substituted for the source's benefited wording.

relationship: standing before God for the good of opponents
rationale: Jeremiah 15 appeals to having stood before the Lord in a time of affliction for good toward the enemy. Jeremiah 18 similarly asks God to remember the prophet's standing before Him to speak good for people who plotted against his life. Both contrast intercession for others with hostility received from them.

relationship: treasures handed over as plunder
rationale: Jeremiah 15 announces treasures given as plunder in connection with sins throughout the borders. Jeremiah 20 likewise announces the city's strength and Judah's royal treasures given into enemy hands and carried to Babylon. The connection concerns the explicit loss of resources; the preceding fragment about iron is not reconstructed.

relationship: exile to an unfamiliar land
rationale: Jeremiah announces enslavement to enemies in an unfamiliar land. Deuteronomy likewise warns that the people and rulers will be led to a nation neither they nor their fathers knew, where service follows. Both describe removal into foreign domination; the target explicitly names service to other gods.

relationship: fire kindled from divine wrath
rationale: Jeremiah's warning of enslavement adds that fire kindled from the Lord's fury will burn upon the people. Deuteronomy likewise describes fire kindled from His wrath and its consuming reach. The shared origin and burning action connect the two judgment images.

relationship: reproach borne on God's account
rationale: Jeremiah asks for remembrance and vindication while saying he received reproach concerning the Lord. The psalmist likewise says he endured reproach on God's account and bears the reproaches directed against Him. Both place the speaker's persecution within his relationship to God.

relationship: God's word as the heart's rejoicing
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord's word will become rejoicing and his heart's joy amid rejection and reproach. The psalmist calls God's testimonies the heart's rejoicing. The shared delight in divine speech supports the connection; Jeremiah's supplied unit does not say that the prophet ate the words.

relationship: refusal to sit with an improper assembly
rationale: Jeremiah says he did not sit in the others' playful gathering but sat alone in reverence and bitterness. The psalmist likewise denies sitting with an empty council or the ungodly assembly. Both describe deliberate separation from a gathering, while Jeremiah adds the particular cost of solitude.

relationship: unreliable water as an image of suffering and disappointment
rationale: Jeremiah describes a persistent wound and compares the experience to false water without faithfulness. Job compares the failure of those nearest him to a failing winter torrent and melting snow, followed by abandonment. Both use unreliable-water imagery to express suffering and disappointment; Job explicitly identifies failed human support, while Jeremiah's referent remains less explicit.

relationship: commission to serve as God's mouth
rationale: Jeremiah 15 promises that, upon return and the separation of honored from unworthy, the prophet will be as the Lord's mouth. Jeremiah's initial commission places the Lord's words in his mouth and appoints him over nations and kingdoms. The later conditional promise recalls the concrete speaking commission without removing its condition.

relationship: repeated promise of a bronze wall and rescue
rationale: Both passages make Jeremiah a fortified or strong bronze wall against the people and rulers, say that opponents will fight but not prevail, and ground deliverance in the Lord's presence. The repeated image and assurances directly connect the renewed promise to his earlier commission.

relationship: rescue from the hand of wrongdoers
rationale: The Lord promises to rescue and ransom Jeremiah from evil and pestilent people's hands. The psalm says the Lord guards His holy ones' souls and rescues them from sinners' hands. Both express protection from hostile human power through the same hand-and-rescue image.

relationship: marriage counsel under distress
rationale: Jeremiah receives a specific command not to take a wife in the setting of the coming disaster described in the following verses. Paul likewise counsels not seeking a wife because of present distress, while explicitly saying marriage is not sin. The connection concerns marriage under crisis and preserves the different scope of command and counsel.

relationship: same-chapter reason for the prophetic family sign
rationale: The statement that no son or daughter will be born to Jeremiah is followed by an oracle concerning the area's children and parents and their impending death. The adjoining passage explains why the prophet's own family life becomes a sign of that particular catastrophe.

relationship: dead people exposed to birds and beasts
rationale: Jeremiah 16 announces unburied and unmourned deaths, with people becoming an example upon the land and prey for beasts and birds. Jeremiah 7 likewise says the people's dead will feed heaven's birds and the earth's beasts with no one driving them off. Both depict the denial of protective burial through exposure to animal consumption.

relationship: prophet forbidden ordinary mourning as a sign
rationale: Jeremiah is told not to enter mourning or lament because the Lord has removed peace from the people. Ezekiel is likewise instructed not to perform ordinary mourning and then reports his wife's death and obedience. Both make restricted prophetic mourning part of a judgment sign, though their personal circumstances differ.

relationship: mourning incisions as a named practice
rationale: Jeremiah predicts that no mourning cuts will be made for the dead. Leviticus prohibits incisions in the body for a dead person. The law identifies the same funerary practice named in the oracle; Jeremiah's prediction of its absence is not turned into a new legal command.

relationship: baldness made for the dead
rationale: Jeremiah says the people will not shave themselves in mourning. Deuteronomy prohibits making a bald place between the eyes for the dead. Both name bodily hair removal in a funerary setting, with a more specific bodily location in the law and a prediction in the oracle.

relationship: absence of consoling food and ordinary mourning
rationale: Jeremiah says bread will not be broken for consolation over the dead and no consoling cup will be given. Ezekiel's announcement of family loss likewise excludes eating the bread of men and ordinary mourning. The comparison concerns the interruption of funerary consolation; Ezekiel does not mention Jeremiah's cup.

relationship: same-chapter banquet prohibition and its explanation
rationale: The prophet is forbidden to sit with the people in a house of eating and drinking. The following because-clause explains that the Lord will stop joy, rejoicing and marriage voices from that place. The particular social prohibition functions as a sign of the announced end of communal celebration.

relationship: repeated cessation of joy and marriage voices
rationale: Both oracles announce that the Lord will stop the sounds of joy and gladness and the voices of bridegroom and bride in the people's cities or place. Jeremiah 7 adds the desolation of the land, giving an earlier occurrence of the same judgment refrain.

relationship: question about why the Lord brought disaster
rationale: Jeremiah anticipates the people's question about the evils announced against them and the wrongdoing behind them. Deuteronomy likewise anticipates questions about the Lord's anger against the land, answered by covenant abandonment and foreign worship. Both use a question-and-answer pattern to explain disaster through prior disobedience.

relationship: ancestral covenant abandonment and foreign worship
rationale: Jeremiah explains the announced disaster through the fathers' abandonment of the Lord, service to foreign gods and failure to keep His law. Deuteronomy gives the corresponding explanation of forsaking the ancestral covenant and serving other gods. The relationship is the explicit cause assigned to judgment.

relationship: present disobedience exceeding the fathers' pattern
rationale: Jeremiah accuses the current people of doing worse than their fathers and following their own evil hearts rather than obeying. Jeremiah 7 likewise says repeated prophetic sending was answered by refusal to hear and a neck hardened beyond the fathers. Both emphasize continuation and intensification of the ancestral refusal.

relationship: unfamiliar exile and service to other gods
rationale: Jeremiah announces removal to a land unknown to the people and fathers, where they will serve other gods without mercy. Deuteronomy warns of removal to a nation unknown to them and their fathers and service there to gods of wood and stone. The destination's unfamiliarity and the religious service are both explicit.

relationship: repeated replacement of the exodus oath formula
rationale: Jeremiah 16 says the coming oath will no longer refer simply to the Lord bringing Israel from Egypt; the following unit names the new return. Jeremiah 23 repeats that movement from the Egyptian exodus to gathering from northern and other lands. The full target preserves the replacement's positive half as necessary context.

relationship: repeated gathering from northern and scattered lands
rationale: Both passages describe the Lord bringing Israel from the northern land and all the regions of dispersion and restoring the people to their land. The close wording links two statements of the promised return in this edition's native chapter order.

relationship: return from dispersion to ancestral land
rationale: Jeremiah promises return from every region of displacement to the land given to the fathers. Deuteronomy promises gathering from the nations and the ends of heaven and return to the land the fathers inherited. The passages share the geographical reversal from dispersion to ancestral possession.

relationship: judgment pursuit leaving no hiding place
rationale: Jeremiah announces fishermen and then hunters who pursue people on mountains, hills and in rock openings. Amos likewise describes divine pursuit of fugitives even on Carmel's summit, in sea depths or in captivity. Both portray an inescapable search in a judgment setting; Jeremiah's fishing is not treated as a mission to gather disciples.

relationship: divine sight includes every way and wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord's eyes are upon all the people's ways and their wrongs are not hidden. Proverbs says His eyes are in every place, observing both evil and good people. Both explicitly connect the reach of divine sight with moral conduct.

relationship: double recompense for sins
rationale: Jeremiah announces repayment of double for the people's injustices and sins. Isaiah's consolation says Jerusalem has received double for her sins from the Lord's hand. The shared measure connects an announcement of recompense with a proclamation that suffering is fulfilled, without supplying an independent chronology between the oracles.

relationship: nations turning from useless idols to the saving Lord
rationale: Jeremiah anticipates nations coming from the earth's extremity and confessing that their inherited idols are false and useless. Isaiah gathers those saved from the nations, contrasts wooden images unable to save with the only saving God, and calls the earth's extremity to turn to Him. The movement from failed idols to the Lord corresponds.

relationship: nations coming to acknowledge the unique God
rationale: Jeremiah says nations will come to the Lord and recognize the falsehood of inherited idols. The psalm likewise anticipates all nations coming to bow before and glorify Him because He alone is the great God. Both envision the nations' acknowledgment of divine uniqueness.

relationship: human manufacture cannot produce a useful god
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether a human will make gods and says the resulting objects are not gods. Isaiah calls those fashioning gods futile and their carved products useless. Both challenge the divine status or benefit claimed for things humans manufacture.

relationship: God's power makes His name known
rationale: Jeremiah announces that the Lord will show His hand and power so that people know His name is Lord. Exodus joins deliverance by an uplifted arm and great judgment to the promise that Israel will know He is the Lord their God. Both connect recognition of His name with an enacted display of His power.
